Reciprocal-Tail Rigidity: Complete Reasoning Record

Erdős #243 45 pp Equations typeset from the exact TeX
PDFOpen the PDF · 45 pp TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis

A claim-bounded complete reasoning record for Erdős #243. It retains the centred-state dynamics, negative-mass recovery, bounded-rise and periodic exclusions, conditional bounded-negative result, residue mechanisms, and all registered families. Mixed-sign unbounded negative excursions remain uncontrolled, so the original eventual-recurrence problem remains open.

This paper owns the complete problem-specific reasoning surface for Erdős #243, including all registered result families and their boundaries.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #243, which remains open.

Introduction

Sylvester’s sequence 2,3,7,43,1807,…2,3,7,43,1807,… is generated by 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1 and has reciprocal sum 11; the recurrence is equivalent to the telescoping identity

1𝑎𝑛−1−1=1𝑎𝑛−1+1𝑎𝑛−1.1an−1−1=1an−1+1an−1.

Consequently the tail beginning with 1/𝑎𝑛−11/an−1 equals 1/(𝑎𝑛−1 −1)1/(an−1−1). Erdős Problem #243 asserts that this is the only way a sequence of that growth can have a rational reciprocal sum:

Problem 1 (Erdős #243). Let 1 ≤𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯1≤a1<a2<⋯ be a sequence of integers with

lim𝑛→∞𝑎𝑛𝑎2𝑛−1=1and∑1𝑎𝑛∈ℚ.limn→∞anan−12=1and∑1an∈Q.

Then 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

See [4] and [5]. Bloom’s catalogue records the problem as open [8]. Below we index the same recurrence as 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1, which is the shift the formal sources use; the two forms are the same statement. Write syl⁡(𝑎) =𝑎2 −𝑎 +1syl⁡(a)=a2−a+1, the Sylvester successor.

The hypothesis is asymptotic and the conclusion is exact. Clearing a rational tail as 𝐶𝑛/𝐷𝑛Cn/Dn exposes that distinction in the integer 𝐸𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛En=Dn−(an−1)Cn: a Sylvester tail has 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0, while quadratic growth only gives 𝐸𝑛/𝐶𝑛 →0En/Cn→0. Integrality alone cannot turn this relative estimate into 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 when 𝐶𝑛Cn grows. The exact dynamics retain extra information: old divisors persist, and they constrain which numerator heights the orbit can visit. This is the arithmetic information used by the bounded-negative and record-crossing arguments.

Section 2 carries out that conversion at one prescribed rate and settles the assertion of Problem 1 on the resulting class of sequences. Section 3 places the theorem against the published sufficient conditions, states the evidence class of every result here, and guides the rest of the note.

Keywords. irrationality; Ahmes series; Sylvester’s sequence; unit fractions; Lean 4. MSC 2020. 11J72 (primary); 11B37, 11D68, 68V20 (secondary).

An unconditional irrationality theorem

The short note treats the cubic-rate theorem as a further consequence. This section supplies its full polynomial and number-field argument. The canonical integer state is constructed first; the general error coordinates are developed in Section 4.

Theorem 2 (cubic-rate irrationality). If strictly increasing positive integers satisfy 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3), then ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛∑n1/an is irrational.

Theorem 3 (rising-factorial cubic exclusion). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℤ>0a,C,D:N→Z>0 satisfy

𝐶𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛−𝐷𝑛,𝐷𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛.(1)(1)Cn+1=anCn−Dn,Dn+1=anDn.

Then for every 𝐴 ∈ℚ>0A∈Q>0 and every 𝐵 ∈ℚB∈Q,

lim inf𝑋→∞#{𝑛≤𝑋:𝐶𝑛≠𝐴𝑛(𝑛+1)(𝑛+2)+𝐵}𝑋>0.lim infX→∞#{n≤X:Cn≠An(n+1)(n+2)+B}X>0.

In particular no such orbit satisfies 𝐶𝑛 =𝐴 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2) +𝐵Cn=An(n+1)(n+2)+B for all large 𝑛n.

The quantifier in Theorem 3 is the one that the irrationality theorem needs. It excludes agreement along prefixes whose proportion of exceptions tends to zero, along every subsequence of prefix lengths, which is more than the exclusion of eventual equality. The two restrictions that meet on the same cubic are integrality, which supplies the rising-factorial shape and the scale, and the denominator transport, which imposes an arithmetic square condition; the scale calculation and the two residue words that close the argument can be checked on the page.

Evidence.

Ordinary proof. The finite claims are the two words (14) and (15), the image {0,2,5,6}{0,2,5,6} of the first-step recursion modulo 77, the divisor condition (𝑟2 +𝑠2)2 ∣48(r2+s2)2∣48, and the countermodel 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2) +( −1)𝑛n(n+1)(n+2)+(−1)n; all four are displayed above and replayed exactly. No Lean declaration covers Theorem 2 or Theorem 3; the centred-coordinate form of Lemma 12 rests on the defect identity, which is kernel-checked. Lemma 7 uses the Chebotarev density theorem in its finite-Galois form and no effective or unproved input.

Position.

Theorem 2 carries no rationality hypothesis and no state hypothesis, and it is the only unconditional irrationality statement in this note. Its rate class lies inside the growth hypothesis of Problem 1, because 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3) forces 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1. On that class the assertion of Problem 1 therefore holds, by exclusion of a rational reciprocal sum, and the recurrence is never exhibited; Sylvester’s own sequence, whose ratio 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1an2/an+1 is 1 +𝑂(1/𝑎𝑛)1+O(1/an), lies outside the class. The rate 1 +3/𝑛1+3/n sits strictly beyond the two sufficient hypotheses recorded in Section 3: it fails Koizumi’s 1 +𝑜(1/𝑛)1+o(1/n) condition, and ∑𝑛𝛾𝑛∑nγn diverges, so Duverney’s convergent-defect hypothesis does not apply. Theorem 3 is independent of any growth or positivity assumption on (𝑎𝑛)(an) beyond (1), and the later sections of this note decide nothing at the cubic rate.

Prior work, and the status of the note

Two published sufficient conditions.

Two published results reach the original problem under analytic hypotheses that are assumed nowhere in this note. Their hypotheses are conditions on the sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an) itself. Duverney’s is not comparable with the state-level hypotheses used here; the Erdős–Straus one, read through the dictionary of the next paragraph, is implied by nonnegativity of 𝐸E, the hypothesis of Theorem 37, so that criterion already covers the descent of Section 8 (see ). Erdős and Straus proved that if lim𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1 =1liman/an−12=1, the reciprocal sum is rational, and 𝑎𝑛an does not satisfy the recurrence, then

lim sup𝑛→∞ [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛]𝑎𝑛+1(𝑎2𝑛+1𝑎𝑛+2−1)>0,lim supn→∞ [a1,…,an]an+1(an+12an+2−1)>0,

where [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛][a1,…,an] is the least common multiple [1]. This is the indexing in the original theorem. Erdős’s 1988 survey, followed by the current catalogue summary, instead prints 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1an2/an+1−1 in the second factor while retaining the same prefix-LCM quotient; that displayed summary is off by one and is not followed here [5][8]. Koizumi records the convenient sufficient rate 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +𝑜(1/𝑛)an2/an+1=1+o(1/n) under which the Erdős–Straus criterion settles the problem [7].

Duverney proved a conditional signed form of the problem itself: for signs 𝜖𝑛 ∈{ −1,1}ϵn∈{−1,1}, if ∑𝑛≥0(𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 −1)∑n≥0(an+1/an2−1) converges, then the reciprocal sum with numerators 𝜖𝑛ϵn is rational if and only if

𝑎𝑛+1=𝑎2𝑛−(𝜖𝑛+1/𝜖𝑛)𝑎𝑛+𝜖𝑛+2/𝜖𝑛+1an+1=an2−(ϵn+1/ϵn)an+ϵn+2/ϵn+1

for all large 𝑛n [2]. Absolute convergence is a stronger sufficient specialisation, not the hypothesis printed in that corollary. The all-positive specialisation is the form relevant here.

Badea’s positive-term criterion is adjacent but different: for positive rational terms 𝑏𝑛/𝑎𝑛bn/an, eventual strict inequality

𝑎𝑛+1>𝑏𝑛+1𝑏𝑛𝑎2𝑛−𝑏𝑛+1𝑏𝑛𝑎𝑛+1an+1>bn+1bnan2−bn+1bnan+1

forces irrationality, while rationality under the corresponding non-strict inequality forces eventual equality [3]. These positive-term hypotheses do not cover the mixed-sign state orbits studied here. Neither result is formalised here, and the results below do not recover either of them.

Koizumi’s work on doubly exponential sequences [7] bears directly on the state system used below, and supplies the coordinates in which several of the statements of this note are most naturally read. For a rational 𝑟 =𝑝/𝑞r=p/q with pseudo-greedy expansion (𝑎𝑛)(an), remainders (𝑥𝑛)(xn) and gap sequence 𝜀𝑛 =𝑥−1𝑛 +1 −𝑎𝑛εn=xn−1+1−an, his Lemma 4  [7] produces integers 𝑐𝑛 >0cn>0, 𝑑𝑛dn and 𝑒𝑛en with 𝑥𝑛 =𝑐𝑛/𝑑𝑛xn=cn/dn and 𝜀𝑛 =𝑒𝑛/𝑐𝑛εn=en/cn, satisfying

𝑎𝑛=𝑑𝑛−𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑛+1,𝑐𝑛+1=𝑐𝑛−𝑒𝑛,𝑑𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑛,an=dn−encn+1,cn+1=cn−en,dn+1=andn,

and the proof of that lemma also gives 𝑐𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑛 −𝑑𝑛cn+1=ancn−dn. Under the dictionary (𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐸𝑛) =(𝑐𝑛,𝑑𝑛,𝑒𝑛)(Cn,Dn,En)=(cn,dn,en) these are exactly the objects of Section 4: the first relation is the centring map ctrctr rewritten as 𝑒𝑛 =𝑑𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝑐𝑛en=dn−(an−1)cn, the second is Proposition 13, the third is the denominator update, and the fourth is the tail update. The lower-case 𝑒𝑛en of Section 4 is −𝐸𝑛−En, so it is the negative of Koizumi’s 𝑒𝑛en at an index where the centred state is negative.

His Theorem 3  [7] shows that his Conjecture 6, that for a positive rational 𝑟r whose gap sequence satisfies 𝜀𝑛 →0εn→0 one has 𝜀𝑛 =0εn=0 for all large 𝑛n, is equivalent to an affirmative answer to the question of Erdős and Graham recorded as his Question 5, which is Problem 1 above. Two of the implications proved below have prior art in these canonical coordinates: his Lemma 3, that 𝜀𝑛 =0εn=0 forces 𝜀𝑛+1 =0εn+1=0, is the absorption of Theorem 22, and his Proposition 1(2), that 𝜀𝑛 ≥0εn≥0 for all large 𝑛n forces 𝜀𝑛 =0εn=0 for all large 𝑛n, is the descent of Theorem 37. These appear in canonical coordinates in [7]. Koizumi attributes Proposition 1(2) to Badea. Its contrapositive says that a counterexample must have negative errors infinitely often; it assumes the sign is eventually nonnegative, while Theorem 48 below assumes only that the negative part is eventually bounded, which admits sign changes of bounded depth at every scale.

The growth hypothesis in Problem 1 is calibrated by two facts about Sylvester’s sequence. It satisfies 𝑎𝑛 ≈𝑐2𝑛0an≈c02n with 𝑐0 =1.2640847…c0=1.2640847…, and shifting it further produces sequences with 𝑎𝑛 ≈𝐶2𝑛an≈C2n for arbitrarily large 𝐶C whose reciprocals still sum to a rational number [6]. The classical sufficient condition for irrationality, lim𝑛𝑎1/2𝑛𝑛 =∞limnan1/2n=∞, is therefore sharp. Kovač and Tao identify that condition as folklore  [6]; they attribute the sharpness observation to Erdős (1975). A sequence with 𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1 →1an/an−12→1 has 𝑎1/2𝑛𝑛an1/2n convergent, so that criterion says nothing about the sequences of Problem 1, and rationality is genuinely possible there. Sylvester’s sequence is A000058 in the OEIS and its shifts A129871. For the recent literature on irrationality of Ahmes series we refer to Kovač and Tao [6], who resolve several problems of Erdős and Graham drawn from the same two sources cited above, and whose introduction gives a sample of the intermediate work, including Sándor (1984) and Badea (1987). They do not treat Problem #243; the rigidity conclusion asked for there is not among their results.

The Formal Conjectures collection contains a mathematically equivalent unproved declaration, up to its zero-based indexing  . Its summand is ℚQ-valued, so Lean’s Summable hypothesis asserts the existence of a sum in ℚQ; the finite indexing shift changes that sum only by a rational prefix. The declaration therefore does encode the rationality premise, but its proof is sorry. Its role here is statement-level prior art; it supplies no proof authority, and the development in this note is independent of it. The machine-checked results concern the state system: they exclude constant and periodic negative magnitudes, the bounded-rise barrier of Theorem 43, and the two conditional endpoints (Theorems 48 and 50), each stated with the exact hypotheses that separate it from Problem #243.

Strongest result. If strictly increasing positive integers satisfy 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3), then ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛∑n1/an is irrational (Theorem 2). The theorem assumes that rate and nothing else. The rate class sits inside the growth hypothesis of Problem 1, so the assertion of the problem holds on it, by exclusion of a rational reciprocal sum; the recurrence is never exhibited. This is an ordinary proof with an exact finite replay, given in full in Section 2, and no Lean declaration covers it.

Strongest statement under the problem’s own hypotheses. Under the hypotheses of Problem 1 and no others, the sequence is eventually Sylvester if and only if the weighted record-excess sum ∑𝑛∈R( −𝑉𝑛 −𝐵)+𝑓(𝑈𝑛)∑n∈R(−Vn−B)+f(Un) is finite for some integer 𝐵 ≥0B≥0 (Theorem 24). This is an ordinary proof whose finite first-crossing arithmetic is kernel-checked and whose analytic half is not. The hypotheses of Problem 1 do not supply that finiteness, so the criterion is a target-equivalent reformulation of the problem rather than a solution of it.

Strongest Lean-checked result. Under the exact integer dynamics, positivity, normalised vanishing, and an eventually bounded negative part, the centred error 𝐸𝑛En is eventually zero. The original sequence therefore satisfies the Sylvester recurrence from some point onward (Theorem 48), in the bounded-negative-part recurrence theorem (boundedNegativePart_sylvesterNext_eventually is not in this checkout). Hypothesis (5), the bound on the negative part, is supplied by nothing in this note.

Second endpoint. The same conclusion holds when the normalised negative mass ∑𝑛( −𝐸𝑛)+/𝐶𝑛∑n(−En)+/Cn is finite, provided the strict centred-step equation is available (Theorem 50).

What remains open. Koizumi’s coordinates provide normalised vanishing for the canonical orbit, but they do not provide either bounded negative excursions or finite normalised negative mass. Any surviving counterexample must therefore have cofinally unbounded negative excursions and divergent normalised negative mass (Proposition 52), record increments strictly above the log-log scale (Theorem 25), and unbounded record-amplified error (Theorem 27).

Proof spine. The record criterion charges each first crossing of a CRT-selected height to the record excess at the step that crosses it, and the crossing heights carry a divergent weight. For the state-system endpoints, bounded negative errors control the rise of the integer tail state; a gcd stabilisation reduces the orbit to pairwise-coprime fresh moduli, and a block of consecutive multiples then gives the contradiction. The finite-mass argument replaces the uniform bound by a summable recovery estimate.

The remaining exclusions sharpen this boundary. By Theorem 22, a counterexample has 𝐸𝑛 ≠0En≠0 for every large 𝑛n. By Theorem 37 it cannot have 𝐸E eventually nonnegative. If its tail is all negative, Theorems 39 and 40 exclude, respectively, constant magnitude and periodic magnitude in the stated regime 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an with positive drift; they are not a classification of a mixed-sign tail. Under normalised vanishing, Theorems 48 and 50 show that the negative part is neither bounded nor of finite normalised mass. What survives is stated in Section 14.

Structure

Section 2 proves the unconditional cubic-rate irrationality theorem, which is the only result here that settles the assertion of Problem 1 on a class of sequences. Section 4 sets up the state system, and Section 5 proves the defect identity, from which eventual vanishing of 𝐸E forces the Sylvester recurrence and a single vanishing error propagates. Section 6 then proves the exact record-excess criterion, and Section 7 states the further criteria in the record coordinates. Section 8 disposes of the case 𝐸 ≥0E≥0 in three lines. The rest of the note is the case 𝐸 <0E<0, in four widening steps: constant magnitude (Section 9), periodic magnitude (Section 10), bounded magnitude via a coprimality barrier (Sections 11 and 12), finite normalised negative mass (Section 13), and what is left (Section 14). These sections contain the new content; a reader who wants only the strongest statements should read Section 2, then Sections 6 and 7, and then Section 14. Appendix 15 is a guide to the formal sources, and Appendix 16 records an exact residue reduction that an earlier finite search used. Linked phrases open the corresponding Lean declaration at the pinned source revision 92b88dc1bbe0. Where a section names a Lean module that is outside that revision, it says so in place of a link.

The centred integer state

The three maps defined next carry out the two steps announced at the end of Section 1. The first two clear denominators along the sequence, so that a rational reciprocal sum leaves a sequence of integers; the third subtracts from that integer the value it takes on Sylvester’s sequence, leaving one number whose vanishing is the whole question. All three are maps between integer tuples and carry no hypothesis of any kind.

For 𝑎,𝐷,𝐶 ∈ℤa,D,C∈Z define

den⁡(𝑎,𝐷)=𝑎𝐷,tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)=𝑎𝐶−𝐷,ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)=𝐷−(𝑎−1)𝐶,den⁡(a,D)=aD,tail⁡(a,D,C)=aC−D,ctr⁡(a,D,C)=D−(a−1)C,

the denominator update, the tail update, and the centred state. Given a sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an) of integers, whose terms we call the multipliers, we write 𝐷𝑛+1 =den⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Dn+1=den⁡(an,Dn) for the denominator state, 𝐶𝑛+1 =tail⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)Cn+1=tail⁡(an,Dn,Cn) for the tail state, and 𝐸𝑛 =ctr⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)En=ctr⁡(an,Dn,Cn) for the centred state, also called the error. The word centred records what the third map does: it measures 𝐷𝑛Dn against (𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛(an−1)Cn, and 𝐷𝑛 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛Dn=(an−1)Cn holds at every index on Sylvester’s sequence (Example 14), so 𝐸E is a deviation from that sequence rather than a size. At an index where 𝐸𝑛 <0En<0 we write 𝑒𝑛 = −𝐸𝑛 >0en=−En>0 and call it the magnitude of the error there.

Proposition 13 (update law). tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶) =𝐶 −ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)tail⁡(a,D,C)=C−ctr⁡(a,D,C); that is, 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 −𝐸𝑛Cn+1=Cn−En.

Proof. 𝐶 −(𝐷 −(𝑎 −1)𝐶) =𝑎𝐶 −𝐷C−(D−(a−1)C)=aC−D. ◻

Formalised as the update law. The state therefore moves by exactly the error at each step, which is what makes the sign of 𝐸E decisive: where 𝐸E is positive the state falls, where 𝐸E is negative it rises, and where 𝐸E vanishes it is stationary.

Let 𝑇𝑛 =∑𝑘≥𝑛1/𝑎𝑘Tn=∑k≥n1/ak and suppose 𝑇0 ∈ℚT0∈Q. Put 𝐷0D0 equal to a common denominator and 𝐷𝑛 =𝐷0𝑎0⋯𝑎𝑛−1Dn=D0a0⋯an−1, and set 𝐶𝑛 =𝐷𝑛𝑇𝑛Cn=DnTn. The Lean module carries no rationality hypothesis and no growth hypothesis; it proves identities and implications about the integer system above, and about its natural-number realisation, for which the bridging identities are the tail realisation, the denominator realisation, and the signed update law.

The series itself is reached by three further declarations, which were absent from earlier revisions of this note. Write 𝐶𝑛/𝐷𝑛Cn/Dn for the real ratio carried by the natural state, the tail ratio. Given 𝑎𝑛 >0an>0, 𝐷𝑛 >0Dn>0, 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn, one exact step removes 1/𝑎𝑛1/an from that ratio one-step reciprocal identity, finite iteration telescopes to a partial sum plus the endpoint ratio finite telescoping, and convergence of the endpoint ratio to zero identifies the infinite sum the series realisation: ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛∑n1/an then has sum 𝐶0/𝐷0C0/D0. These three carry no growth hypothesis, no centring hypothesis and no rationality hypothesis, and they exclude nothing. They close the loop between the integer system and the series that motivates it. Producing the state of a given rational sum, which is the direction the problem needs, is the exposition of this paragraph and is not a checked statement.

Proposition 15 (scale equivariance). For every 𝑠,𝑎,𝐷,𝐶 ∈ℤs,a,D,C∈Z,

den⁡(𝑎,𝑠𝐷)=𝑠den⁡(𝑎,𝐷),tail⁡(𝑎,𝑠𝐷,𝑠𝐶)=𝑠tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶),den⁡(a,sD)=sden⁡(a,D),tail⁡(a,sD,sC)=stail⁡(a,D,C),

This is used twice below: once to normalise the finite search of Appendix 16, and once, in Theorem 40, as the induction step that removes common scale.

The defect identity and its two consequences

Section 4 connects the Sylvester recurrence to the error in one direction only: on Sylvester’s sequence the error vanishes. The converse is what the problem needs, and it comes from a single identity, which expresses the deviation of 𝑎𝑛+1an+1 from the Sylvester successor, multiplied by the tail state 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1, as a combination of the errors at 𝑛n and at 𝑛 +1n+1, the first weighted by 𝑎2𝑛an2. Its two consequences are Theorem 21, in which an eventually vanishing error forces the recurrence provided the tail state is eventually nonzero, and Theorem 22, in which, under strict centring (the condition |𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛|En|<Cn at every index), one vanishing error propagates to every later index.

Write def⁡(𝑎,𝑎′) =𝑎′ −syl⁡(𝑎)def⁡(a,a′)=a′−syl⁡(a) for the deviation of the next term from the Sylvester successor, the Sylvester defect.

Theorem 16 (defect identity). For all 𝑎,𝑎′,𝐷,𝐶 ∈ℤa,a′,D,C∈Z,

def⁡(𝑎,𝑎′)⋅tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)=𝑎2ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)−ctr⁡(𝑎′,den⁡(𝑎,𝐷),tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)),def⁡(a,a′)⋅tail⁡(a,D,C)=a2ctr⁡(a,D,C)−ctr⁡(a′,den⁡(a,D),tail⁡(a,D,C)),

that is, Δ𝑛 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛𝐸𝑛 −𝐸𝑛+1ΔnCn+1=an2En−En+1.

Two-step cancellation and feedback

The one-step state equations hide a second-order constraint once the raw numerator is reduced at two consecutive stages. Write 𝑢,𝑢1,𝑢2u,u1,u2 for the primitive numerator coordinates, 𝑣,𝑣1v,v1 for the corresponding denominator coordinates, and ℎ,ℎ1h,h1 for the two common factors removed in reduction. If the two steps have multipliers 𝑎,𝑎1a,a1, then the exact hypotheses are

ℎ𝑢1+𝑣=𝑎𝑢,ℎ𝑣1=𝑎𝑣,ℎ1𝑢2+𝑣1=𝑎1𝑢1.hu1+v=au,hv1=av,h1u2+v1=a1u1.

Proof. Multiply the first equation by 𝑎a, replace 𝑎𝑣av using the second equation, and then replace ℎ1𝑢2 +𝑣1h1u2+v1 using the third. The remaining terms factor as the displayed right-hand side. ◻

This is the two-step primitive recurrence. The hard point is keeping both changing cancellation factors visible. The result is stronger than a one-step congruence, though it remains non-autonomous and cannot by itself force 𝑎1 =𝑎2 −𝑎 +1a1=a2−a+1.

𝑝2+𝑎2𝑝=(𝑎+𝑎1)𝑝1.p2+a2p=(a+a1)p1.

Then

Theorem 20 (cancellation-free curvature identity). Let 𝑎,𝑎1,𝑝,𝑝1,𝑝2,𝑞a,a1,p,p1,p2,q be integers with 𝑞 =𝑎𝑝 −𝑝1q=ap−p1 and 𝑝2 +𝑎2𝑝 =(𝑎 +𝑎1)𝑝1p2+a2p=(a+a1)p1. Then

𝑞2+(𝑝𝑝2−𝑝21)=(𝑎1−𝑎)𝑝𝑝1.q2+(pp2−p12)=(a1−a)pp1.

The square 𝑞2q2 is the local remainder, while 𝑝𝑝2 −𝑝21pp2−p12 is a discrete curvature term. The right side records the change in multiplier, so the identity supplies a diagnostic for an anti-shadowing argument without asserting a sign or a global monotonicity. It is checked as the cancellation-free curvature square; no global anti-shadowing conclusion is claimed.

Finally, the reduced denominator transport has a precise realizability gate. Let 𝑒,𝑒1e,e1 be centred errors and let ΔΔ be the Sylvester defect. If

ℎ𝑢1=𝑢−𝑒,ℎ𝑒1=𝑎2𝑒−Δ(𝑢−𝑒),hu1=u−e,he1=a2e−Δ(u−e),

then the transport equality

has mismatch which factors through 𝑢 −𝑒u−e. Consequently, when 𝑢 −𝑒 ≠0u−e≠0,

ℎ((𝑎1−1)𝑢1+𝑒1)=𝑎((𝑎−1)𝑢+𝑒)⟺𝑎1=𝑎2−𝑎+1+Δ.h((a1−1)u1+e1)=a((a−1)u+e)⟺a1=a2−a+1+Δ.

This is the exact feedback transport equivalence, obtained from the factored defect at feedback transport defect. The nonzero-raw-numerator hypothesis is essential: if 𝑢 −𝑒 =0u−e=0, the factorised mismatch cannot identify 𝑎1a1.

These three identities require orbit-level hypotheses that remain unproved: eventual absence of cancellation, a fixed sign for the curvature, or cofinal passage through the feedback gate. The global mixed-sign and unbounded-negative regimes of Problem #243 remain open.

Theorem 21 (sequence form). Let 𝑎,𝐷,𝐶 :ℕ →ℤa,D,C:N→Z satisfy 𝐷𝑛+1 =den⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Dn+1=den⁡(an,Dn) and 𝐶𝑛+1 =tail⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)Cn+1=tail⁡(an,Dn,Cn). If 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n and 𝐶𝑛+1 ≠0Cn+1≠0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n, then 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Formalised as the eventual Sylvester recurrence. The proof is routine: take the larger of the two thresholds and apply Theorem 18 at each later index. Every later section is directed at the hypothesis of this theorem, that is, at forcing 𝐸E to vanish eventually.

The defect identity has a second consequence, which is what makes a single vanishing error worth having.

Theorem 22 (zero is absorbing). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N be an exact natural orbit, so 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn, and let 𝐸𝑛 =ctr⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)En=ctr⁡(an,Dn,Cn). Suppose the centring is strict, |𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛|En|<Cn for every 𝑛n. If 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 then 𝐸𝑛+1 =0En+1=0.

Proof. Putting 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 in Theorem 16 gives Δ𝑛𝐶𝑛+1 = −𝐸𝑛+1ΔnCn+1=−En+1, so 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1 divides 𝐸𝑛+1En+1. A multiple of 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1 of absolute value smaller than 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1 is zero, and |𝐸𝑛+1| <𝐶𝑛+1|En+1|<Cn+1 by hypothesis. ◻

Formalised as the absorption of a vanishing centred state, with the companion contrapositive along a tail: if zero is absorbing beyond some index and 𝐸E does not vanish eventually, then 𝐸E is nowhere zero beyond that index.

Absorption changes the shape of the problem. Either 𝐸E hits zero once and stays there, or it is never zero. Sections 9 and 10 address the special all-negative case only. The mixed-sign analysis in Sections 12 and 13 instead separates cofinally negative errors from an eventually positive tail.

Weighted first crossings of LCM records

This section recovers the weighted record criterion used by the short note. It is an exact criterion for Problem 1, stated under the hypotheses of that problem and no others, and it is reached by a first-crossing argument rather than by a hypothesis on the negative part. Only steps setting a new LCM numerator record contribute, a fixed LCM-scale baseline may be subtracted, and the remaining mass may be logarithmically discounted.

Evidence.

The result in this section is an ordinary mathematical proof. Its finite arithmetic and charging steps are kernel-checked at an immutable source revision: the freshness of a rise, the covered-wall excess bound, the wall count, and the weighted wall charge. The global analytic argument, which is the passage from the per-step charge to divergence of the whole sum, is not formalised. An exact finite replay covers 6,0086,008 seed-modulus cases over 6,0006,000 distinct rational seeds, 26,17126,171 nonterminal transitions and 6,0086,008 terminal states, and every case reaches centred zero within 1515 steps; finite data of that kind do not prove universal termination.

What the record coordinates transfer.

The criterion moves the obligation off the whole orbit. Only steps setting a new LCM numerator record contribute, a fixed LCM-scale baseline may be subtracted, and the remaining mass may be logarithmically discounted, so a counterexample has to sustain divergence along a sparse subsequence. The inherited part of the picture is the eventual regime 𝐸𝑛 ≥0En≥0, which Koizumi’s Proposition 1(2) closes, and to which the published sign criteria apply once the shift of Proposition 35 is subtracted. What is added here is a criterion valid in the complementary regime as well, stated under the hypotheses of Problem 1 and no others. Two propositions bound what these coordinates reach. Proposition 35 exhibits cancellation-free blocks on which every classical hypothesis quantity fails by a fixed number of units, and Proposition 36 shows that the data used by Theorem 43 and the landing lemmas admit walks with rises of order ℓ(𝑢)ℓ(u), so an argument using only those data excludes no negative part of that order. A producer that closes the gap has to enter the regime displayed in Section 7, where the negative part is at least (1 −𝛿)log2⁡log2⁡𝐶𝑛(1−δ)log2⁡log2⁡Cn and is 𝑜(𝐶𝑛)o(Cn) at infinitely many indices, and inside that regime it has to use the congruence 𝐸𝑛 ≡𝐷𝑛(mod𝐶𝑛)En≡Dn(modCn) beyond coprimality, or supply a second mechanism that forces landings.

Remaining obligation.

Derive finiteness of the displayed sum for one admissible weight and one fixed 𝐵B from rational denominator feedback, or contradict a nonterminal orbit by another route. The logarithmic discount weakens what suffices; it does not establish it.

Criteria in the record coordinates

The criterion of Section 6 lives in the LCM coordinates 𝑈𝑛 =𝐶𝑛/𝑀𝑛Un=Cn/Mn, where old divisors persist. The statements of this section live in the primitive coordinates, where old divisors can be deleted. They are collected here because each is an equivalence, a dichotomy, or an unconditional exclusion, and because each sharpens the profile of a counterexample in a direction the earlier sections do not reach.

Primitive coordinates.

The record-increment coefficient

Theorem 25 (record-excess dichotomy). Let Θ =lim sup𝑛(𝐻𝑛+1 −𝐻𝑛)/ℓ(𝐻𝑛)Θ=lim supn(Hn+1−Hn)/ℓ(Hn) on a nonterminating canonical orbit under (H). Mechanism.

Four steps. The drawdown ladder 𝑟𝑛 =( −𝐸𝑛 −𝐵𝑛)+rn=(−En−Bn)+ with 𝐵𝑛+1 =(𝐵𝑛 +𝐸𝑛)+Bn+1=(Bn+En)+ and 𝐵𝑛 =𝐻𝑛 −𝐶𝑛Bn=Hn−Cn gives 0 ≤𝑟𝑛 ≤( −𝐸𝑛)+0≤rn≤(−En)+, so a bound on the record increment is weaker than a bound on the negative error and is therefore the better trigger. Proof. The interval [𝑥,𝑥 +𝐿)[x,x+L) contains exactly 𝐿L integers. Each lies in [1,∞)[1,∞) and is smaller than 𝑥 +𝐿x+L, so a modulus exceeding 𝑥 +𝐿x+L divides none of them. Each of the 𝑘k remaining moduli divides at most 𝐿/𝑚𝑖 +1L/mi+1 of them, so the covered count is at most 𝐿𝜃 +𝑘 <𝐿Lθ+k<L.

𝑘(𝑦+1+𝐿(𝑦))1−𝜃≤ℓ(𝑦)+𝐶+𝑜(1)1−𝜃<𝜌ℓ(𝑦)≤𝐿(𝑦),k(y+1+L(y))1−θ≤ℓ(y)+C+o(1)1−θ<ρℓ(y)≤L(y),

while 𝐿(𝑦) ≤(1 +𝜖)ℓ(𝑦)L(y)≤(1+ϵ)ℓ(y). Starting with 𝑢0u0 sufficiently large, apply the first part with 𝑥 =𝑢𝑛 +1x=un+1 and length 𝐿(𝑢𝑛)L(un), and choose 𝑢𝑛+1un+1 in the resulting window. The sequence is strictly increasing, avoids every retained modulus, and has the required rise bound. ◻

The integer hypotheses are used in the first sentence of the proof. For example, the real interval [99.1,100.2)[99.1,100.2) has length 1.11.1 but contains only the integer 100100; a covered count smaller than 1.11.1 need not leave an uncovered integer.

Reading.

Theorem 43 and the landing lemmas use about the multipliers only that they are pairwise coprime, that they divide later denominator states, and that a modulus dividing the current numerator is impossible at a landing, which is whole-modulus avoidance. Proposition 36 shows that those data admit walks whose rises reach (1 +𝜖)ℓ(𝑢𝑛)(1+ϵ)ℓ(un), so the bounded-rise hypothesis of Theorem 43 cannot be relaxed to a rise of order ℓ(𝑢)ℓ(u) by any argument using only them, and the constant 11 in Corollary 26 is the CRT constant rather than a feature of the problem. Coprimality to 𝑚𝑖mi is a strictly stronger requirement than avoiding its multiples, and the window statement is false for it: the pairwise coprime family 30,31,931,…30,31,931,… has ∑𝑖1/𝑚𝑖 =1/15∑i1/mi=1/15, and no integer of [2,5)[2,5) is coprime to 3030. Ordinary proof, with a numerical witness walk whose maximal rise against Sylvester’s numbers as moduli is 1212 up to height 2 ⋅1062⋅106, and whose maximal ratio (𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛)/ℓ(𝑢𝑛)(un+1−un)/ℓ(un) against the Fermat moduli 22𝑗 +122j+1 is 1.81161.8116 for 𝑢 ≥1000u≥1000 up to 3 ⋅1063⋅106. The Fermat product ∏𝑗≥0(1 −1/(22𝑗 +1))∏j≥0(1−1/(22j+1)) telescopes to 1/21/2 exactly; whether that constant is the exact maximal-gap coefficient is Problem 58.

The exact remaining obstacle.

Every criterion of this section leaves the same regime, which is

(1−𝛿)ℓ(𝐶𝑛) ≤ −𝐸𝑛 = 𝑜(𝐶𝑛)at infinitely many 𝑛,(1−δ)ℓ(Cn) ≤ −En = o(Cn)at infinitely many n,

with divergent normalised negative mass, unbounded record-amplified error, and infinitely many clean primitive record jumps of size at least three. Any argument entering it must use the congruence 𝐸𝑛 ≡𝐷𝑛(mod𝐶𝑛)En≡Dn(modCn) beyond coprimality, or supply a second mechanism that forces landings.

Descent when the error is nonnegative

The hypothesis of the theorem below is the update law of Proposition 13 read inside ℕN: the error is nonnegative at every index, so the tail state never rises. This is the easy case, and it is settled in three lines.

Theorem 37 (descent). Let 𝐶,𝐸 :ℕ →ℕC,E:N→N satisfy 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐸𝑛 =𝐶𝑛Cn+1+En=Cn for every 𝑛n. Then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Proof. A one-line descent. The relation forces 𝐶𝑛+1 ≤𝐶𝑛Cn+1≤Cn, so 𝐶C is a nonincreasing sequence of natural numbers and is eventually equal to its minimum; beyond that index 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛Cn+1=Cn, and the relation gives 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0. ◻

Formalised as the stabilisation of the nonnegative error, on the eventual constancy of a nonincreasing sequence.

The hypothesis is exactly one-sidedness: 𝐶C and 𝐸E take values in ℕN. If 𝐸𝑛 <0En<0 at infinitely many indices then 𝐶C rises there, nothing descends, and the argument is unavailable. That is the whole difficulty, and the rest of this note is directed at it.

Excluding a constant negative magnitude

Suppose the error is negative with a constant magnitude, 𝐸𝑛 = −𝑚En=−m for a fixed 𝑚 >0m>0 and every 𝑛n. By Proposition 13 the state then climbs by exactly 𝑚m each step, so 𝐶𝑛 =𝑐 +𝑛𝑚Cn=c+nm with 𝑐 =𝐶0c=C0, and the definition of the centred state becomes a shape equation

𝐷𝑛+𝑚=(𝑎𝑛−1)(𝑐+𝑛𝑚).(5.1)(5.1)Dn+m=(an−1)(c+nm).

Together with 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn this is a closed system in (𝑎,𝐷)(a,D), and it has no solutions. The following instance shows how the failure happens; the theorem then shows that it cannot be avoided.

Example 38 (the shape equation running until it fails). Take 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1, so that 𝐶𝑛 =1 +𝑛Cn=1+n and the shape equation (5.1) reads 𝐷𝑛 +1 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)(1 +𝑛)Dn+1=(an−1)(1+n), and take 𝐷0 =1D0=1. Each step is now determined: at 𝑛 =0n=0 the equation reads 2 =(𝑎0 −1) ⋅12=(a0−1)⋅1, so 𝑎0 =3a0=3, and 𝐷1 =𝑎0𝐷0 =3D1=a0D0=3; at 𝑛 =1n=1 it reads 4 =(𝑎1 −1) ⋅24=(a1−1)⋅2, so 𝑎1 =3a1=3, and 𝐷2 =𝑎1𝐷1 =9D2=a1D1=9; at 𝑛 =2n=2 it reads 10 =(𝑎2 −1) ⋅310=(a2−1)⋅3, which has no integer solution, and the orbit stops. Longer prefixes occur for other starting values: the finite search recorded in Appendix 16 found none longer than 1717 among the initial states below 50005000.

Theorem 39 (no constant negative magnitude). There is no pair of sequences 𝑎,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,D:N→N with 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2 for all 𝑛n satisfying 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn and (5.1), for any 𝑚 >0m>0 and any 𝑐c. The same holds if the shape only begins at some index.

Proof when 𝑐c and 𝑚m are coprime. Assume first gcd(𝑐,𝑚) =1gcd(c,m)=1. Two facts about the multipliers do all the work, and the difficulty lies in the fact that they concern the same finite set of primes from opposite directions: the first makes every multiplier meet that set, the second lets each prime of the set meet at most one multiplier.

Every 𝑎𝑗aj shares a prime with 𝑚m. Suppose gcd(𝑎𝑗,𝑚) =1gcd(aj,m)=1. Then 𝑚m is invertible modulo 𝑎𝑗aj, so some 𝑛n has 𝑐 +𝑛𝑚 ≡0c+nm≡0, that is 𝑎𝑗 ∣𝐶𝑛aj∣Cn; and 𝑎𝑗 ∣𝐷𝑛aj∣Dn for every 𝑛 >𝑗n>j, since 𝐷D is multiplicative with 𝑎𝑗aj among its factors. Choosing such an 𝑛n beyond 𝑗j and reading (5.1) modulo 𝑎𝑗aj gives 𝑎𝑗 ∣𝑚aj∣m, contradicting gcd(𝑎𝑗,𝑚) =1gcd(aj,m)=1 and 𝑎𝑗 ≥2aj≥2.

A prime divisor of 𝑚m occurs in at most one 𝑎𝑗aj. Suppose 𝑝 ∣𝑚p∣m and 𝑝 ∣𝑎𝑗p∣aj. For 𝑛 >𝑗n>j we have 𝑝 ∣𝐷𝑛p∣Dn, so (5.1) gives (𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛 ≡0(mod𝑝)(an−1)Cn≡0(modp). Now 𝐶𝑛 =𝑐 +𝑛𝑚 ≡𝑐Cn=c+nm≡c, and 𝑝 ∤𝑐p∤c because 𝑝 ∣𝑚p∣m and gcd(𝑐,𝑚) =1gcd(c,m)=1; hence 𝑝 ∣𝑎𝑛 −1p∣an−1, so 𝑝 ∤𝑎𝑛p∤an. Thus 𝑝p cannot divide any later multiplier.

The two facts are incompatible. Each of the infinitely many multipliers needs a prime divisor of 𝑚m, and each prime divisor of 𝑚m serves at most one multiplier, while 𝑚m has only finitely many prime divisors. ◻

The case gcd(𝑐,𝑚) =1gcd(c,m)=1 is the scale-primitive exclusion. The special case 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1, worked through in Example 38, where 𝑚m has no prime divisors at all and the first fact is immediately contradictory, is recorded separately as the normalised exclusion.

Removing the scale. For general 𝑐c, put 𝑔 =gcd(𝑐,𝑚)g=gcd(c,m). Equation (5.1) shows 𝑔 ∣𝐷𝑛g∣Dn for every 𝑛n, so dividing 𝐷D, 𝑐c and 𝑚m by 𝑔g leaves a system of the same shape with coprime data, which the previous case excludes. ◻

Formalised as the exclusion at every scale, and the eventual form, obtained by shifting the orbit to the first constant index, as the eventual exclusion.

Theorem 39 excludes a centred state that is eventually constant and negative, at every magnitude and every scale. It says nothing about a negative state whose magnitude changes, and the argument genuinely uses constancy: the finiteness of the set of prime divisors of 𝑚m is what the pigeonhole uses, and a varying magnitude presents a fresh set at each index.

Excluding a periodic negative magnitude

The next case allows the magnitude to vary, provided it repeats. Write 𝑒𝑛 = −𝐸𝑛 >0en=−En>0 for the magnitude, as in Section 4, so that 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 +𝑒𝑛Cn+1=Cn+en; suppose 𝑒e has period ℎh, meaning 𝑒𝑛+ℎ =𝑒𝑛en+h=en for every 𝑛n, and that the state gains a fixed drift 𝑀 >0M>0 over one period, meaning 𝐶𝑛+ℎ =𝐶𝑛 +𝑀Cn+h=Cn+M for every 𝑛n.

At ℎ =1h=1 this says that the magnitude is constant and that 𝑀M is its value, which is the situation of Section 9; Theorem 39 already excludes it, and does so without the extra hypothesis 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an imposed below. The new content is ℎ ≥2h≥2.

Section 9 could run its pigeonhole on the prime divisors of the single number 𝑚m. Here the magnitude changes inside a period, and the number available to run it on is the drift 𝑀M. Three lemmas replace the two facts of Section 9. The first is that multipliers persist: every 𝑎𝑗aj divides every strictly later denominator state, the persistence of a multiplier. The second is a lock: a prime already dividing 𝐷D and also dividing the current multiplier is forced into the next tail state, the one-step lock, and once present in both 𝐷D and 𝐶C it stays in every later 𝐷D, 𝐶C and magnitude, the persistence of a lock. The third transports a lock backwards through the period: if a divisor of the drift 𝑀M occurs in two multipliers, it is a common divisor of 𝐶0C0 and of every magnitude, the repeated-divisor transport, using that both the period relation and the drift iterate over any number of periods, the iterated period and the iterated drift.

Theorem 40 (no periodic negative magnitude). Let 𝑎,𝐷,𝐶,𝑒 :ℕ →ℕa,D,C,e:N→N with 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2, 𝑒𝑛 >0en>0 and 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an for every 𝑛n, satisfying

𝐷𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛+1=𝐶𝑛+𝑒𝑛,𝐷𝑛+𝑒𝑛=(𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛,Dn+1=anDn,Cn+1=Cn+en,Dn+en=(an−1)Cn,

and suppose 𝑒𝑛+ℎ =𝑒𝑛en+h=en and 𝐶𝑛+ℎ =𝐶𝑛 +𝑀Cn+h=Cn+M for some ℎ >0h>0 and 𝑀 >0M>0. This is impossible.

Proof. Strong induction on the drift 𝑀M. The difficulty lies in the fact that a repeated prime divisor of 𝑀M need not contradict anything directly. It instead forces a common scale on the whole orbit, which can be divided out, and the induction runs on the drift that the division reduces.

Suppose first that no prime divisor of 𝑀M is a common divisor of 𝐶0C0 and of every magnitude. Repeated-divisor transport then applies in the contrapositive: a prime divisor of 𝑀M occurring in two of the multipliers would be exactly such a common divisor, so each prime divisor of 𝑀M occurs in at most one multiplier. Against this, the argument of Section 9 run phase by phase (along a fixed residue class modulo ℎh the magnitude is constant and 𝐶C advances by 𝑀M at each period, so the multipliers of that phase meet an arithmetic progression exactly as in Section 9) makes every multiplier share a prime with 𝑀M. Since 𝑀M has only finitely many prime divisors and there are infinitely many multipliers, pigeonhole gives a contradiction.

Otherwise some prime 𝑝p divides 𝑀M, divides 𝐶0C0, and divides every magnitude. Then 𝑝 ∣𝐶𝑛p∣Cn for every 𝑛n, since 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 +𝑒𝑛Cn+1=Cn+en and both summands on the right are divisible by 𝑝p, and the shape equation 𝐷𝑛 +𝑒𝑛 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛Dn+en=(an−1)Cn then gives 𝑝 ∣𝐷𝑛p∣Dn for every 𝑛n. Divide 𝐷D, 𝐶C and 𝑒e by 𝑝p. The multipliers are untouched, so 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2 and 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an persist and the magnitudes stay positive; the three recurrences are homogeneous in (𝐷,𝐶,𝑒)(D,C,e) and so survive; the period is still ℎh; and the drift becomes 𝑀/𝑝 <𝑀M/p<M. The inductive hypothesis applies. ◻

The first of the two cases above is the phase-primitive exclusion, the induction is the exclusion at every scale, and the eventual form is the eventual exclusion.

The bound 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an is a genuine restriction and not a normalisation. It is the range in which a multiplier cannot divide its own phase magnitude, which is what the lock argument needs. It holds in the intended reading, where 𝑒𝑛en is a centred representative and 𝑎𝑛an grows quadratically, but it is assumed here and not derived. The drift hypothesis 𝑀 >0M>0 is also used: a periodic magnitude with zero drift would be identically zero, which is the case already settled by Section 8.

Remark 1. On the canonical orbit of , read through the dictionary of Section 3, the bound 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an holds eventually. Lemma 4(2) there gives the centring range −𝐶𝑛/2 ≤𝐸𝑛 <𝐶𝑛/2−Cn/2≤En<Cn/2, so 𝑒𝑛 =|𝐸𝑛| ≤𝐶𝑛/2en=|En|≤Cn/2 at a negative index, and the proof of Lemma 4(3) gives 𝐶𝑛+1 ≤32𝐶𝑛Cn+1≤32Cn  , hence the uniform bound 𝐶𝑛 ≤𝐶0(3/2)𝑛Cn≤C0(3/2)n. Against this, summability of ∑1/𝑎𝑛∑1/an forces 𝑎𝑛 →∞an→∞, and the growth hypothesis 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 →1an2/an+1→1 gives 𝑎𝑛+1 ≥𝑎2𝑛/2an+1≥an2/2 for all large 𝑛n, hence 𝑎𝑛+1 ≥2𝑎𝑛an+1≥2an once 𝑎𝑛 ≥4an≥4; so the multipliers grow at least geometrically with ratio 22 and outgrow the bound on 𝐶𝑛Cn, making 𝑒𝑛/𝑎𝑛en/an eventually small. Two caveats. Summability is used for this step, so the estimate is not available from the state recurrence alone; and the conclusion is eventual and not universal, whereas Theorem 40 imposes 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an at every index, so it is the eventual form of the exclusion cited above that applies. Under the periodicity hypothesis of Theorem 40 the estimate is in any case unnecessary, since a periodic magnitude is bounded while the multipliers tend to infinity.

Bounded rise cannot remain coprime to fresh moduli

Periodicity is still a strong assumption. Removing it needs a different kind of obstruction, and the one used here is a counting argument about where an integer sequence with bounded upward steps must land.

Lemma 41 (shifted blocks of consecutive multiples). Let 𝑚0,…,𝑚𝐵−1m0,…,mB−1 be pairwise coprime and at least 22. For every bound there is a 𝑡t beyond it with 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑡 +𝑖mi∣t+i for each 𝑖 <𝐵i<B.

Proof. Standard Chinese remaindering: solve 𝑡 ≡ −𝑖(mod𝑚𝑖)t≡−i(modmi) simultaneously, then add multiples of ∏𝑖𝑚𝑖∏imi to pass the bound. ◻

Formalised as the shifted consecutive multiples.

Example 42 (a block of three consecutive multiples). Take 𝐵 =3B=3 and (𝑚0,𝑚1,𝑚2) =(3,4,5)(m0,m1,m2)=(3,4,5). The congruences 𝑡 ≡0(mod3)t≡0(mod3), 𝑡 ≡3(mod4)t≡3(mod4) and 𝑡 ≡3(mod5)t≡3(mod5) hold exactly when 𝑡 ≡3(mod60)t≡3(mod60). At 𝑡 =3t=3 the block is 3,4,53,4,5 with 3 ∣33∣3, 4 ∣44∣4 and 5 ∣55∣5; at 𝑡 =63t=63 it is 63,64,6563,64,65 with 3 ∣633∣63, 4 ∣644∣64 and 5 ∣655∣65. A sequence of natural numbers that starts at 00, tends to infinity and rises by at most 33 at each step cannot step over the block {3,4,5}{3,4,5}: it has a first value at least 33, that value is at most 55, and every member of {3,4,5}{3,4,5} is divisible by one of the three moduli.

Theorem 43 (bounded rise cannot remain coprime to fresh moduli). Let 𝑢 :ℕ →ℕu:N→N tend to infinity with 𝑢𝑛+1 ≤𝑢𝑛 +𝐵un+1≤un+B for a fixed 𝐵 >0B>0. Then 𝑢u cannot remain coprime to infinitely many fresh pairwise coprime moduli: there is no family of pairwise coprime 𝑚𝑖 ≥2mi≥2, one for each index, such that gcd(𝑚𝑖,𝑢𝑡) =1gcd(mi,ut)=1 whenever 𝑖 <𝑡i<t.

The time threshold in the proof is essential. The rise bound restricts upward jumps but permits arbitrary falls: for example, if 𝑀 ≥1M≥1, then 𝑢0 =𝑀u0=M, 𝑢1 =0u1=0, and 𝑢𝑛 =𝑛 −1un=n−1 for 𝑛 ≥1n≥1 satisfies the bound with 𝐵 =1B=1 and tends to infinity, although the large height 𝑀M is already attained at time 00.

Proof. Choose 𝑚0,…,𝑚𝐵−1m0,…,mB−1 and use Lemma 41 to find 𝑡 >max(𝑢0,…,𝑢𝐵)t>max(u0,…,uB) with 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑡 +𝑖mi∣t+i for 0 ≤𝑖 <𝐵0≤i<B. Since 𝑢𝑛 →∞un→∞, there is a first 𝑛 >𝐵n>B with 𝑢𝑛 ≥𝑡un≥t. Minimality and the rise bound give

𝑡≤𝑢𝑛≤𝑢𝑛−1+𝐵<𝑡+𝐵.t≤un≤un−1+B<t+B.

Hence 𝑢𝑛 =𝑡 +𝑖un=t+i for some 0 ≤𝑖 <𝐵 <𝑛0≤i<B<n, so 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑢𝑛mi∣un. The inequality 𝑖 <𝑛i<n now permits the avoidance hypothesis, which says gcd(𝑚𝑖,𝑢𝑛) =1gcd(mi,un)=1; this contradicts 𝑚𝑖 ≥2mi≥2. The argument uses the first crossing of the CRT block, not monotonicity of 𝑢u. ◻

Formalised as the bounded-rise barrier. The key point is that the two hypotheses pull against each other exactly: divergence forces 𝑢u to travel arbitrarily far, and bounded rise forbids it from stepping over a window of width 𝐵B. Uniformity of the bound is what the proof uses, and it is the hypothesis that cannot be relaxed by this argument: a rise bounded only along a subsequence leaves the intervening steps free to jump the window. We have not looked for a sequence of unbounded rise remaining coprime to every fresh modulus. The statement is elementary and we are not aware of a prior published form of it, but we would not be surprised if one exists.

The moduli are indexed by the same set as the sequence, and the 𝑖ith of them is asked to divide no value 𝑢𝑡ut with 𝑡 >𝑖t>i; nothing at all is asked of it at or before its own index. That asymmetry is what makes the hypothesis available in the application below, where 𝑚𝑖mi is the 𝑖ith multiplier and only the later numerators are known to be coprime to it.

The barrier applies to the problem because a reduced exact tail already carries pairwise coprime moduli. Call (𝑢,𝑣)(u,v) a reduced exact tail with multipliers 𝑎a when gcd(𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛) =1gcd(un,vn)=1,

𝑢𝑛+1+𝑣𝑛=𝑎𝑛𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝑣𝑛.un+1+vn=anun,vn+1=anvn.

Here 𝑢u is the numerator and 𝑣v the denominator: the two recurrences are those of Section 4, with 𝑢u in the role of the tail state 𝐶C and 𝑣v in that of the denominator state 𝐷D, and with coprimality imposed at every index.

Proposition 44 (reduced tails are pairwise coprime). In a reduced exact tail, 𝑎𝑛an is coprime to 𝑣𝑛vn; the multipliers at distinct indices are pairwise coprime; and every earlier multiplier is coprime to every later numerator.

These are the step coprimality, the pairwise coprimality, and the whole-modulus avoidance. Feeding them to Theorem 43 gives the form used later: there is no reduced exact tail whose numerator tends to infinity with a uniformly bounded upward increment, the reduced bounded-rise exclusion, together with its eventual form, the eventual reduced exclusion.

Example 45 (Sylvester’s sequence as a reduced exact tail). Put 𝑢𝑛 =1un=1 and 𝑣𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 =1,2,6,42,1806,…vn=Dn=1,2,6,42,1806,… as in Example 14, with multipliers 𝑎𝑛 =𝑣𝑛 +1 =2,3,7,43,1807,…an=vn+1=2,3,7,43,1807,…. Then gcd(𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛) =1gcd(un,vn)=1, 𝑢𝑛+1 +𝑣𝑛 =1 +𝑣𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝑢𝑛un+1+vn=1+vn=anun and 𝑣𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝑣𝑛vn+1=anvn, so this is a reduced exact tail, and Proposition 44 returns the classical fact that Sylvester’s numbers are pairwise coprime. Its numerator is constant, so it satisfies every hypothesis of the exclusion just stated except divergence; since the tail exists, that hypothesis cannot be dropped.

An arbitrary orbit of Section 4 need not be reduced, so one more step is needed before the barrier can be applied to it: the common factor must stop changing. We call a set of indices cofinal when it is infinite, and say that a property holds cofinally when the set of indices at which it holds is cofinal. The step below is the only one connecting the orbit of Section 4 to the reduced tails of Proposition 44, and it is where the cofinal boundedness in the proof of Theorem 48 is used.

Proposition 46 (the tail gcd stabilises). Let (𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)(a,D,C) be an exact natural orbit, that is, a triple of ℕN-valued sequences with 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn, whose centred state 𝐸𝑛 =ctr⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)En=ctr⁡(an,Dn,Cn) is negative cofinally, with magnitudes bounded along that cofinal set. Then gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)gcd(Cn,Dn) is eventually constant, and beyond that index the orbit divided by the stable gcd is a reduced exact tail.

Proof. The tail gcd gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)gcd(Cn,Dn) divides its successor, the gcd monotonicity, so the tail gcds form a positive divisibility chain. At an index where the centred state is negative the tail gcd is exactly gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝑒𝑛)gcd(Cn,en), the gcd at a negative index, and is therefore at most the magnitude there; so the chain is bounded along the cofinal set of negative indices. A positive divisibility chain whose values are bounded along a cofinal set is eventually constant, the chain stabilisation. Hence cofinally bounded negative magnitudes make the tail gcd stabilise, the gcd stabilisation, and beyond that point dividing by the stable gcd leaves the numerator and denominator coprime, that is, a reduced exact tail. ◻

The stabilisation of the tail gcd is the checked statement cited at the end of the proof; the last clause, that the divided orbit is a reduced exact tail, is exposition and carries no separate label. Boundedness is required only along a cofinal set. That is what the situation gives: the tail gcd is controlled only at the negative indices, and cofinally many of them is all the divisibility chain needs.

Normalised vanishing by itself gives a different, strictly weaker conclusion. For an exact natural orbit with 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, put

Proposition 47 (normalised vanishing makes strict gcd changes sparse). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N satisfy 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn with 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, and put 𝐸𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛En=Dn−(an−1)Cn, 𝐺𝑛 =gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Gn=gcd(Cn,Dn) and Γ(𝑁) =#{0 ≤𝑗 <𝑁 :𝐺𝑗 <𝐺𝑗+1}Γ(N)=#{0≤j<N:Gj<Gj+1}. The first assertion is the sublinear strict-growth theorem; the second is the arbitrarily late constant-block theorem. The proof first converts normalised vanishing into subexponential growth of 𝐶𝑛Cn, then charges every strict divisibility increase of 𝐺𝑛Gn against a finite power-of-two budget. Sparse strict changes force long finite gaps between them.

The quantifiers matter. Proposition 46 uses cofinally bounded negative magnitudes and yields eventual constancy. Proposition 47 uses only normalised vanishing and yields arbitrarily late constant blocks of each prescribed finite length. It does not yield one infinite constant tail, and it does not exclude cofinally unbounded negative excursions.

Excluding a bounded negative part

Assembling the previous section gives Theorem 48, the endpoint of the barrier argument. Theorem 50 in the next section uses a different finiteness hypothesis. The two results are incomparable: Theorem 50 assumes only the state recurrence with 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, while hypothesis (5) below does not imply finite normalised negative mass, by which we mean convergence of ∑𝑛( −𝐸𝑛)+/𝐶𝑛∑n(−En)+/Cn, where 𝑥+ =max(𝑥,0)x+=max(x,0), since a constant negative part −𝑏−b gives 𝐶𝑛 ∼𝑏𝑛Cn∼bn and hence a divergent sum. The hypotheses of Theorem 48 are listed in full, because two of them are analytic inputs that are assumed here rather than derived from the growth condition of Problem 1.

Informally, hypotheses (5) and (6) below pull against each other. By Proposition 13, hypothesis (5) caps the rise of the tail state at 𝐵B per step, while hypothesis (6), once the error is nowhere zero, forces the tail state to diverge. Proposition 46 makes the orbit reduced, and Theorem 43 then converts the tension into a contradiction: an integer sequence tending to infinity with upward steps of size at most 𝐵B cannot remain coprime to the pairwise coprime moduli a reduced tail carries. The complementary case, in which the error is eventually positive, is the descent of Theorem 37.

Then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Proof. Suppose not. We first remove every late zero: by Theorem 22 and its contrapositive form, 𝐸E is nowhere zero beyond the centring threshold. Two cases remain. If 𝐸E is negative cofinally, then (5) bounds those magnitudes, so Proposition 46 makes the tail gcd stabilise and the orbit may be taken reduced past that point. Hypothesis (5) with Proposition 13 gives 𝐶𝑛+1 ≤𝐶𝑛 +𝐵Cn+1≤Cn+B, a bounded rise; hypothesis (6) with 𝐸E nowhere zero gives 𝐶𝑛 →∞Cn→∞. A reduced exact tail with a divergent numerator and bounded rise is excluded by Theorem 43. It remains to treat the case that 𝐸E is eventually positive, and there the descent of Theorem 37 applies and forces 𝐸E to vanish, contradicting nowhere-vanishing. ◻

Formalised as the bounded-negative-part rigidity, with the eventual form, in which the centring and the bound need only hold from some index, as the eventual bounded-negative-part rigidity. The two auxiliary results it uses are the divergence from normalised vanishing and the exclusion of cofinally bounded negative magnitudes, the latter over the tail-divergence form.

Complements and further questions

Problem #243 is open. The negative case has narrowed, and it is worth being precise about what is left.

Each exclusion holds only in its stated regime. Theorems 39 and 40 exclude the constant and the stated periodic magnitudes on an all-negative tail, and do not exclude those patterns merely along the negative indices of a mixed-sign tail; Theorem 48 excludes a bounded negative part under normalised vanishing, and Theorem 50 excludes finite normalised negative mass with no normalised-vanishing hypothesis. Together with absorption and descent they fix the profile of any counterexample.

Proposition 52 (frontier profile for a counterexample). For the canonical integer state attached to any counterexample to Problem 1,

𝐸𝑛≠0eventually,|𝐸𝑛|𝐶𝑛⟶0,En≠0eventually,|En|Cn⟶0,

Fix 𝐾,𝑟,𝐿 ∈ℕK,r,L∈N with 𝐾,𝐿 >0K,L>0, assume

𝐾|𝑒𝑟+𝑖|<𝑢𝑟+𝑖(0≤𝑖<𝐿),𝑢𝑟≤𝑢𝑟+𝐿,K|er+i|<ur+i(0≤i<L),ur≤ur+L,

and let 𝑅R be a finite family of moduli. Suppose every 𝑚𝑞mq, 𝑞 ∈𝑅q∈R, divides the deletion product ∏𝑟≤𝑛<𝑟+𝐿𝑐𝑛∏r≤n<r+Lcn, and that 𝑐2𝑛 ∣ℎ𝑛cn2∣hn throughout the interval. Then

𝐾𝐿lcm⁡(𝑚𝑞:𝑞∈𝑅)2<(𝐾+1)𝐿.(22)(22)KLlcm⁡(mq:q∈R)2<(K+1)L.

This is the repair-entropy inequality.

The square in (22) is the key point. Exact denominator reduction charges 𝑐2𝑛cn2 to the scale growth, so a repaired family whose LCM is at least 2|𝑅|2|R| satisfies

𝐾𝐿4|𝑅|<(𝐾+1)𝐿.KL4|R|<(K+1)L.

The formal consequence is the independent-repair cardinality bound. It rules out positive-density deletion of independent old moduli inside recoveries with a fixed relative-error budget.

There is also an endpoint that does not mention a chosen modulus family. If 𝐾|𝑒𝑛| <𝑢𝑛K|en|<un eventually for every 𝐾K, then for each fixed 𝐿 >0L>0 there is an 𝑁N such that every recovery 𝑢𝑟 ≤𝑢𝑟+𝐿ur≤ur+L with 𝑟 ≥𝑁r≥N satisfies

∏0≤𝑖<𝐿ℎ𝑟+𝑖=1.∏0≤i<Lhr+i=1.

Thus a surviving nontrivial reset must have recovery length tending to infinity. Lean checks this as eventual disappearance of fixed-length reset payments. The theorem does not bound a recovery length that varies with 𝑟r, nor does it supply a lower bound for the LCM of the moduli repaired in such an interval. Those are the missing inputs needed to turn (22) into a global contradiction.

Problem 54 (global overlap-height growth). For every nonterminal canonical orbit satisfying Problem 1, must

lim sup𝑛→∞log⁡𝑀𝑛𝑛>0?lim supn→∞log⁡Mnn>0?

Equivalently, must there be a 𝐾 ≥1K≥1 for which

2𝑛≤𝑀𝐾𝑛2n≤MnK

at infinitely many indices?

The two displayed formulations are equivalent up to changing the positive constant; the second is not a weaker target. On the canonical orbit, Section 6 supplies 𝑀𝑛 ∣𝐶𝑛Mn∣Cn and 𝑀𝑛 ≤𝐶𝑛Mn≤Cn. Therefore a positive answer would contradict the subexponential tail-height budget and prove Problem #243. The missing input is the proposed lower bound on overlap growth.

There is also a more local-looking question whose content is nevertheless the entire prefix. Put 𝐴𝑛 =∏𝑗<𝑛𝑎𝑗An=∏j<naj, so 𝐷𝑛 =𝐷0𝐴𝑛Dn=D0An. From

𝐷0𝐴𝑛=(𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛+𝐸𝑛D0An=(an−1)Cn+En

one immediately obtains

gcd(𝐴𝑛,𝑎𝑛−1)∣𝐸𝑛.gcd(An,an−1)∣En.

The checked tail-height estimate and normalised vanishing make |𝐸𝑛||En| subexponential in 𝑛n.

Problem 55 (old-factor overlap). In every nonterminal canonical orbit satisfying Problem 1, is

lim sup𝑛→∞log⁡gcd(𝐴𝑛,𝑎𝑛−1)𝑛>0?lim supn→∞log⁡gcd(An,an−1)n>0?

Equivalently, do there exist 𝜂 >0η>0 and infinitely many 𝑛n such that gcd(𝐴𝑛,𝑎𝑛 −1) ≥𝑒𝜂𝑛gcd(An,an−1)≥eηn?

A positive answer contradicts the displayed divisibility and the subexponential error budget. Arbitrarily long locally admissible blocks do not answer this question: the gcd uses the complete prefix.

The direct analytic question

Problem 56 (summability from rationality). Let (𝑎𝑛)(an) satisfy Problem 1, and let (𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛,𝐸𝑛)(Dn,Cn,En) be its canonical integer state. Must

∞∑𝑛=0𝛿𝑛=∞∑𝑛=0(−𝐸𝑛)+𝐶𝑛<∞?∑n=0∞δn=∑n=0∞(−En)+Cn<∞?

An affirmative answer closes Problem #243 by Theorem 50. Since 𝛿𝑛 →0δn→0, convergence is equivalently expressible as boundedness of the partial products ∏𝑛<𝑁(1 +𝛿𝑛)∏n<N(1+δn); this is the same criterion in multiplicative form. A negative answer requires a sequence satisfying the full growth and rationality hypotheses. A locally admissible state orbit is insufficient. By Theorem 24, it is enough to establish the finiteness of (20) for one decreasing weight with divergent integral and one fixed baseline. This replaces the all-index mass by a discounted series supported only at LCM records.

Remark 3. One further question is not left open here, since it is answered in [7]: whether normalised vanishing follows from 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1 and rationality. It does. After deleting a finite prefix, Koizumi’s Corollary 3  [7] makes the sequence the pseudo-greedy expansion of its own reciprocal sum and gives 𝜀𝑛 →0εn→0 under exactly the hypotheses of Problem 1; rationality is not needed for that step, only summability of ∑1/𝑎𝑛∑1/an. Since 𝜀𝑛 =𝐸𝑛/𝐶𝑛εn=En/Cn under the intended reading of Section 4, this is normalised vanishing. Strict centring comes from the same source and is stronger than what Theorem 48 assumes: for a rational reciprocal sum, the range −𝑐𝑛/2 ≤𝑒𝑛 <𝑐𝑛/2−cn/2≤en<cn/2 of his Lemma 4(2)  [7] gives |𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛|En|<Cn at every index, which is stronger than eventual strict centring. The eventual form also follows directly from normalised vanishing with 𝐾 =1K=1. What remains unsupplied is hypothesis (5), the bound on the negative part, which is why the theorem is still conditional.

A barrier extension

Problem 57 (variable-rise CRT barrier). Determine the weakest growth condition on the positive increments of 𝑢𝑛un under which an unbounded integer sequence cannot remain coprime to infinitely many pairwise-coprime old moduli as in Theorem 43. In particular, does the conclusion remain valid under the candidate condition

(𝑢𝑛+1−𝑢𝑛)+=𝑜(log⁡log⁡(𝑢𝑛+3))?(un+1−un)+=o(log⁡log⁡(un+3))?

The displayed rate is a proposed threshold, not a proved sharp boundary. Either an extension of the CRT barrier or a counterexample with this rise rate would be informative independently of Problem #243. Proposition 36 bounds the search from above: under whole-modulus avoidance alone the conclusion already fails at the rate (1 +𝜖)ℓ(𝑢𝑛)(1+ϵ)ℓ(un), so the answer lies in the band between 𝑜(ℓ(𝑢𝑛))o(ℓ(un)) and (1 +𝜖)ℓ(𝑢𝑛)(1+ϵ)ℓ(un), and an affirmative answer must use coprimality itself rather than avoidance of multiples.

Problem 58 (the maximal-gap coefficient). Let 𝑚0 <𝑚1 <⋯m0<m1<⋯ be pairwise coprime with ℓ(𝑚𝑗) =𝑗 +𝑂(1)ℓ(mj)=j+O(1) and 𝜎 =∏𝑗(1 −1/𝑚𝑗) >0σ=∏j(1−1/mj)>0, and let 𝑢𝑛un enumerate the integers divisible by no 𝑚𝑗mj. Is lim sup𝑛(𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛)/ℓ(𝑢𝑛) =𝜎−1lim supn(un+1−un)/ℓ(un)=σ−1? For the Fermat moduli 𝑚𝑗 =22𝑗 +1mj=22j+1 the product telescopes to 𝜎 =1/2σ=1/2 exactly, and the observed ratio is 1.81161.8116 for 𝑢 ≥1000u≥1000 up to 3 ⋅1063⋅106 against the proposed value 22.

The upper bound implicit in Proposition 36 is (1 −𝜃)−1(1−θ)−1 with 𝜃 =∑𝑗1/𝑚𝑗θ=∑j1/mj, which for the Fermat family is 2.475…2.475…; the proposed constant 𝜎−1σ−1 is smaller, and no proof of it is offered here.

Formalisation targets

Erdős–Straus.

Formalise Theorem 3 of [1], with its prefix-LCM quotient and correctly indexed growth factor, under the published analytic hypotheses.

Duverney.

Formalise Corollary 3.2 of [2], including its signed numerators and its one-sided summability hypothesis, and then recover the all-positive specialisation used here. These are useful verification projects, but neither is an additional open mathematical problem.

The residue reduction of Appendix 16 is in FiniteHorizonResidue.lean. Three distinctions are worth carrying into the source. The identification of any of these modules with reciprocal tails is the exposition of Section 4 and is not a checked statement. The periodic exclusion assumes the regime 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an. And the final Lean declaration lists strict centring and normalised vanishing as hypotheses; the former follows eventually from the latter with 𝐾 =1K=1, while the formal source derives neither from the original analytic problem. For the external bridge supplying them, see Sections 3 and 12.

A factorial residue reduction for forced orbits

In the case 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1 of Section 9, where the shape equation (5.1) reads 𝐷𝑛 +1 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)(𝑛 +1)Dn+1=(an−1)(n+1), each multiplier is determined by its predecessor; we call such an orbit forced. At index 𝑛n the numerator of the next multiplier is

num⁡(𝑛,𝑎)=(𝑛+1)𝑎2−(𝑛+2)𝑎+(𝑛+3),num⁡(n,a)=(n+1)a2−(n+2)a+(n+3),

the forced numerator, and the divisor is 𝑛 +2n+2. The orbit survives a step when that division is exact, giving a survival predicate, the survival predicate. Example 38 is the forced orbit from 𝑎 =3a=3 read this way: num⁡(0,3) =6num⁡(0,3)=6 is divisible by 22 and gives 𝑎1 =3a1=3, while num⁡(1,3) =13num⁡(1,3)=13 is not divisible by 33, so the orbit stops there. Deciding survival by iteration is expensive because the orbit grows doubly exponentially, and it is unnecessary: survival over a finite horizon depends on the initial value only through a factorial residue.

Theorem 59 (factorial residue reduction). For all ℎh and all integers 𝑎 ≡𝑏(mod(ℎ +1)!)a≡b(mod(h+1)!), the orbit from 𝑎a survives ℎh forced updates exactly when the orbit from 𝑏b does.

Proof. Let 𝑀(0,𝑖) =1M(0,i)=1 and 𝑀(ℎ +1,𝑖) =(𝑖 +2)𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h+1,i)=(i+2)M(h,i+1), an ascending factorial with 𝑀(ℎ,0) =(ℎ +1)!M(h,0)=(h+1)!. The numerator is a polynomial with integer coefficients, so congruences transfer; reducing the modulus gives divisibility by 𝑖 +2i+2 for one exactly when for the other, and cancelling that common factor from both values and modulus leaves the inductive hypothesis at 𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h,i+1). ◻

Formalised as the factorial residue reduction, over the shrinking-modulus transport, the polynomial congruence, and the exact-division cancellation; the modulus identifications are the ascending-factorial form and the factorial value at the initial index.

At ℎ =1h=1 the modulus is 2! =22!=2, and surviving one update means 2 ∣𝑎2 −2𝑎 +32∣a2−2a+3, which holds exactly for odd 𝑎a: for instance num⁡(0,3) =6num⁡(0,3)=6 but num⁡(0,4) =11num⁡(0,4)=11. So one step of survival is decided by the parity of 𝑎a alone, which is Theorem 59 at its smallest nontrivial horizon.

The search this supported is superseded. Running it over initial states below 50005000 produced forced prefixes of length 1717 and no longer; Theorem 39 now excludes the constant-negative case outright, for every seed and at every scale. The reduction is retained because it is exact, and because the shrinking-modulus technique transfers to any forced orbit whose step is a polynomial division.
